claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Cortical magnification is the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm²/°).
claims.source: Cortical magnification –the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm2/°) – declines with eccentricity (Benson et al., 2022; Engel et al., 1994; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Horton and Hoyt, 1991; Van Essen et al., 1984)
claims.evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction.

claims.claim: Cortical magnification declines with eccentricity.
claims.source: Cortical magnification –the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm2/°) – declines with eccentricity (Benson et al., 2022; Engel et al., 1994; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Horton and Hoyt, 1991; Van Essen et al., 1984)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Cortical magnification has been used to link perceptual performance to brain structure.
claims.source: Cortical magnification –the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm2/°) – declines with eccentricity (Benson et al., 2022; Engel et al., 1994; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Horton and Hoyt, 1991; Van Essen et al., 1984) and has been used to link perceptual performance to brain structure (Duncan and Boynton, 2003; Himmelberg et al., 2023a; Himmelberg et al., 2022b; Rovamo et al., 1978; Schwarzkopf et al., 2011; Schwarzkopf and Rees, 2013; Song et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: For many visual tasks, magnifying stimulus size such that the spatial extent of the cortical representation is equated eliminates performance differences at different eccentricities.
claims.source: Indeed, for many visual tasks (e.g., contrast sensitivity, orientation and SF discrimination, grating acuity, temporal frequency sensitivity, and visual search), magnifying stimulus size such that the spatial extent of the cortical representation is equated eliminates performance differences at different eccentricities (Figure 1A; Anton-Erxleben and Carrasco, 2013; Carrasco et al., 1998; Carrasco and Frieder, 1997; Kitterle, 1986; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979; Strasburger et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Grating contrast sensitivity as a function of spatial frequency successfully scales with eccentricity.
claims.source: Particularly relevant to this study, grating contrast sensitivity as a function of SF successfully scales with eccentricity (Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Koenderink et al., 1978; Rovamo et al., 1978; Virsu and Rovamo, 1979).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The decline in performance with eccentricity is due to decreasing neural count with eccentricity (quantitative hypothesis).
claims.source: These studies support a 'quantitative' hypothesis – the hypothesis that the decline in performance with eccentricity is due to decreasing neural count with eccentricity, given that the density, but not distribution, of V1 neurons is approximately uniform across cortex (and thus visual space) (Hubel and Wiesel, 1977; Rockel et al., 1980).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Hubel and Wiesel, 1977 and Rockel et al., 1980.

claims.claim: The density, but not distribution, of V1 neurons is approximately uniform across cortex.
claims.source: These studies support a 'quantitative' hypothesis – the hypothesis that the decline in performance with eccentricity is due to decreasing neural count with eccentricity, given that the density, but not distribution, of V1 neurons is approximately uniform across cortex (and thus visual space) (Hubel and Wiesel, 1977; Rockel et al., 1980).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Hubel and Wiesel, 1977 and Rockel et al., 1980.

claims.claim: The quantitative hypothesis suggests that visual processing is invariant with location; neurons conduct the same computations, regardless of their receptive field position.
claims.source: This hypothesis then suggests that visual processing is invariant with location; neurons conduct the same computations, regardless of their receptive field position.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an implication of the quantitative hypothesis.

claims.claim: Performance does not successfully scale for several visual tasks measuring higher-order dimensions (e.g., numerosity judgments, symmetry detection, and positional relation of image components).
claims.source: Indeed, performance does not successfully scale for several visual tasks measuring higher-order dimensions (e.g., numerosity judgments, symmetry detection, and positional relation of image components; for review, see Strasburger et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Strasburger et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Observers performed an orientation discrimination task with constant stimulus size at different locations.
claims.source: Here, to assess contrast sensitivity, human adult observers performed an orientation discrimination task with constant stimulus size at different locations as well as when stimulus size was M-scaled according to stimulus eccentricity and polar angle location.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Observers performed an orientation discrimination task when stimulus size was M-scaled according to stimulus eccentricity and polar angle location.
claims.source: Here, to assess contrast sensitivity, human adult observers performed an orientation discrimination task with constant stimulus size at different locations as well as when stimulus size was M-scaled according to stimulus eccentricity and polar angle location.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Ten observers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in three conditions.
claims.source: Ten observers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in three conditions (eight females, aged 21–32 y, two authors: MJ and DT).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the participants.

claims.claim: Observers maintained fixation during the task.
claims.source: While maintaining fixation, observers reported the orientation of a target grating for which contrast and spatial frequency (SF) varied on each trial (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: Grating contrast and spatial frequency varied on each trial.
claims.source: While maintaining fixation, observers reported the orientation of a target grating for which contrast and spatial frequency (SF) varied on each trial (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: CSFs decline between the parafovea (2°) and perifovea (6°) for fixed-sized gratings.
claims.source: CSFs decline between the parafovea (2°) and perifovea (6°) for fixed-sized gratings (top row), but differences at low and medium SFs diminish after M-scaling Virsu and Rovamo, 1979 (bottom row).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1 and shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Differences in CSFs at low and medium spatial frequencies diminish after M-scaling.
claims.source: CSFs decline between the parafovea (2°) and perifovea (6°) for fixed-sized gratings (top row), but differences at low and medium SFs diminish after M-scaling Virsu and Rovamo, 1979 (bottom row).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1 and shown in the figure, with citation to Virsu and Rovamo, 1979.

claims.claim: CSFs differ among the horizontal meridian (HM), lower vertical meridian (LVM), and upper vertical meridian (UVM) for fixed-sized stimuli.
claims.source: CSFs differ among the horizontal meridian (HM), lower vertical meridian (LVM), and upper vertical meridian (UVM) for fixed-sized stimuli (top row).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1B and shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Contrast sensitivity peaked at a given spatial frequency and declined more rapidly for higher than lower spatial frequencies.
claims.source: Contrast sensitivity peaked at a given SF and declined more rapidly for higher than lower SFs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the shape of the CSF.

claims.claim: CSFs decreased with eccentricity but less so after M-scaling.
claims.source: CSFs decreased with eccentricity but less so after M-scaling.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The eccentricity effect for fixed-size gratings increased from approximately 30% to 120% across spatial frequency.
claims.source: The eccentricity effect for fixed-size gratings, quantified as the percent change in contrast sensitivity for 2°, 6°, and 6°M-scale, increased from ~30% to 120% across SF (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: After M-scaling, the eccentricity effect became negative for spatial frequencies less than 2 cpd, with higher contrast sensitivity at 6° M-scale than 2°.
claims.source: After M-scaling, the eccentricity effect became negative for SFs <2 cpd, with higher contrast sensitivity at 6°M-scale than 2° (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: M-scaling diminished the eccentricity effect differentially across spatial frequency.
claims.source: A repeated-measures ANOVA (SF: 0.5–11 cpd; stimulus size: fixed vs. M-scaled) showed that M-scaling diminished the eccentricity effect differentially across SF (interaction: F(7,63) = 61.13, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.872).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: M-scaling resulted in significant reductions in contrast sensitivity for spatial frequencies 0.5, 1, 1.4, 2, 2.8, and 4 cpd.
claims.source: Post hoc t-tests revealed significant reductions in contrast sensitivity for all SFs (0.5, 1, 1.4, 2, and 2.8 cpd, p<0.001; 4, cpd, p<0.01) except the two highest SFs (8 and 11 cpd, p>0.1), which reached the acuity limit.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: M-scaling did not result in significant reductions in contrast sensitivity for spatial frequencies 8 and 11 cpd, which reached the acuity limit.
claims.source: Post hoc t-tests revealed significant reductions in contrast sensitivity for all SFs (0.5, 1, 1.4, 2, and 2.8 cpd, p<0.001; 4, cpd, p<0.01) except the two highest SFs (8 and 11 cpd, p>0.1), which reached the acuity limit.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: M-scaling slightly reversed typical eccentricity effects for low spatial frequencies.
claims.source: Thus, consistent with previous results (Rovamo et al., 1978; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979), M-scaling slightly reversed typical eccentricity effects for low SFs and reduced them for medium SFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: M-scaling reduced eccentricity effects for medium spatial frequencies.
claims.source: Thus, consistent with previous results (Rovamo et al., 1978; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979), M-scaling slightly reversed typical eccentricity effects for low SFs and reduced them for medium SFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Contrast sensitivity across spatial frequencies was greater for the horizontal meridian than vertical meridian at 2°, 6°, and 6° M-scale.
claims.source: Contrast sensitivity across SFs was greater for the HM than VM at 2°, 6°, and 6°M-scale (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: At 2° and 6°, the HVA extent increased from 20% to 120% across spatial frequency.
claims.source: At 2° and 6°, the HVA extent increased from 20% to 120% across SF (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Differences in contrast sensitivity between the horizontal meridian and vertical meridian at a fixed eccentricity were as pronounced as tripling stimulus eccentricity from 2° to 6°.
claims.source: Thus, differences in contrast sensitivity between the HM and VM at a fixed eccentricity were as pronounced as tripling stimulus eccentricity from 2° to 6°.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison of the magnitude of HVA to eccentricity effects.

claims.claim: The HVA remained after M-scaling.
claims.source: The HVA remained after M-scaling.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claims.claim: M-scaling the stimulus reduced the HVA extent as a function of spatial frequency.
claims.source: A two-way ANOVA compared its extent at the perifovea (6° eccentricity) before and after M-scaling. M-scaling the stimulus reduced the HVA extent as a function of SF (interaction: F(7,63) = 7.32, p=0.0035, ηG2 = 0.449).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: For all but one spatial frequency (8 cpd), M-scaling did not affect the HVA.
claims.source: For all but one SF (8 cpd: p=0.021, 95% CI = [1.26 57.37], d = 0.75), M-scaling did not affect the HVA (p>0.05).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: Unlike eccentricity, the HVA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification, such as qualitatively different image-processing capabilities and/or neural computations around polar angle.
claims.source: This finding supports the 'qualitative' hypothesis – unlike eccentricity, the HVA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification, such as qualitatively different image-processing capabilities and/or neural computations around polar angle (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the finding that M-scaling does not eliminate the HVA.

claims.claim: Contrast sensitivity across spatial frequencies was higher along the lower vertical meridian than upper vertical meridian for 2°, 6°, and 6° M-scale.
claims.source: Contrast sensitivity across SFs was higher along the LVM than UVM for 2°, 6°, and 6°M-scale (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: For fixed-size and M-scaled gratings, the VMA extent reached a maximum of 40% at 1 cpd in the parafovea and 8 cpd in the perifovea.
claims.source: For fixed-size and M-scaled gratings, the VMA extent reached a maximum of 40% at 1 cpd in the parafovea and 8 cpd in the perifovea.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claims.claim: The VMA has only been characterized at eccentricities greater than 2°.
claims.source: The VMA has only been characterized at eccentricities > 2° (Abrams et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The spatial frequency at which the VMA peaks depends on eccentricity.
claims.source: This near-foveal location reveals that the SF at which the VMA peaks depends on eccentricity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data showing different peak SFs for VMA at different eccentricities.

claims.claim: The VMA remained after M-scaling.
claims.source: The VMA also remained after M-scaling (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: A two-way ANOVA found a main effect of spatial frequency on VMA extent.
claims.source: A two-way ANOVA found a main effect of SF (F(7,63) = 10.16, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.53) due to an increasing perifoveal VMA extent across SF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: There was no main effect of stimulus size on VMA extent.
claims.source: We found neither a main effect of stimulus size nor an interaction effect (p>0.1), indicating no difference in VMA extent before and after M-scaling stimulus size.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: There was no interaction effect between stimulus size and spatial frequency on VMA extent.
claims.source: We found neither a main effect of stimulus size nor an interaction effect (p>0.1), indicating no difference in VMA extent before and after M-scaling stimulus size.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: Unlike eccentricity, the VMA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification, such as distinct neural computations and image-processing capabilities at the upper vertical meridian and lower vertical meridian.
claims.source: This finding further supports the 'qualitative' hypothesis – unlike eccentricity, the VMA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification, such distinct neural computations and image-processing capabilities at the UVM and LVM (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the finding that M-scaling does not eliminate the VMA.

claims.claim: The HVA in peak contrast sensitivity emerged only in the perifovea.
claims.source: The HVA emerged in the peak-CS only in the perifovea (interaction: F(2,18) = 18.33, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.671; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results and shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Peak contrast sensitivity fell between 2° and 6° for both HVA and VMA.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: Peak contrast sensitivity increased in the perifovea after M-scaling for both HVA and VMA.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: Peak contrast sensitivity did not differ between 2° and 6° M-scale.
claims.source: Peak-CS fell between 2° and 6° (HVA: p<0.001, 95% CI = [0.404 0.555], d = 4.52; VMA: p<0.001, 95% CI = [0.513 0.651], d = 6.039), increased in the perifovea after M-scaling (HVA: p<0.001, 95% CI = [-0.639–0.483], d = −5.14; VMA: p<0.001, 95% CI = [-0.681–0.562], d = −7.50), and did not differ between 2° and 6°M-scale (p>0.1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: Differences in peak contrast sensitivity between horizontal meridian and vertical meridian only emerged at 6° and 6° M-scale.
claims.source: Importantly, differences between HM and VM only emerged at 6° (p<0.001, 95% CI = [0.153 0.318], d = 2.04) and 6°M-scale (p<0.01, 95% CI = [0.054 0.175], d = 1.35).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: The VMA in peak contrast sensitivity emerged at 2°, 6°, and 6° M-scale.
claims.source: In contrast, the VMA emerged at 2°, 6°, and 6°M-scale (polar angle main effect: F(1,9) = 8.65, p<0.02, ηG2 = 0.490; Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The HVA emerged in peak contrast sensitivity only in the perifovea, whereas the VMA emerged at both eccentricities.
claims.source: These findings show that the HVA and VMA emerged in peak-CS, but the HVA only in the perifovea, whereas the VMA emerged at both eccentricities.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the findings on peak contrast sensitivity.

claims.claim: M-scaling matched the peak contrast sensitivity between the parafovea and perifovea, but did not equate contrast sensitivity around polar angle.
claims.source: Moreover, although M-scaling matched the peak-CS between the parafovea and perifovea, it did not equate contrast sensitivity around polar angle.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the findings on peak contrast sensitivity.

claims.claim: The HVA and VMA emerged in the cutoff spatial frequency, consistent with previous studies.
claims.source: The HVA and VMA also emerged in the cutoff-SF, consistent with previous studies (Barbot et al., 2021; Wilkinson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: M-scaling reduced the HVA extent in cutoff spatial frequency.
claims.source: M-scaling reduced the HVA extent (interaction: F(2,18) = 19.20, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.681; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results and shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The cutoff spatial frequency decreased between horizontal meridian and vertical meridian at 2°, 6°, and 6° M-scale.
claims.source: The cutoff-SF decreased between HM and VM at 2° (p<0.001, 95% CI = [0.227 0.403], d = 2.56), 6° (p<0.001, 95% CI = [0.231 0.324], d = 4.24), and slightly less so at 6°M-scale (p=0.0326, 95% CI = [0.0251 0.146], d = 1.01).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claims.claim: M-scaling did not eliminate the HVA in cutoff spatial frequency.
claims.source: Thus, M-scaling did not eliminate either the HVA or the eccentricity effect in the cutoff-SF
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the findings on cutoff spatial frequency.

claims.claim: The VMA extent in cutoff spatial frequency only emerged in the perifovea.

claims.claim: Cutoff spatial frequency decreased between the lower vertical meridian and upper vertical meridian at 6° and 6° M-scale.

claims.claim: M-scaling did not eliminate the VMA in cutoff spatial frequency.

claims.claim: M-scaling increased the perifoveal cutoff spatial frequency along the vertical meridian.

claims.claim: The HVA in cutoff spatial frequency occurred at both eccentricities but only in the perifovea for the VMA.
claims.source: In short, the HVA in cutoff-SF occurred at both eccentricities but only in the perifovea for the VMA.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the findings on cutoff spatial frequency.

claims.claim: M-scaling did not equate cutoff spatial frequency among polar angles.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the findings on cutoff spatial frequency.

claims.claim: AULCSF was greater for the horizontal meridian than vertical meridian at 2°, 6°, and 6° M-scale.

claims.claim: The AULCSF for HVA decreased between 2° and 6°.

claims.claim: M-scaling did not eliminate the AULCSF HVA.

claims.claim: AULCSF was greater for the lower vertical meridian than upper vertical meridian at 6° and 6° M-scale, but not at 2°.

claims.claim: The VMA extent in AULCSF decreased from 2° to 6°.

claims.claim: M-scaling did not eliminate the VMA for AULCSF.

claims.claim: The HVA magnitude in peak contrast sensitivity increased between 2° and 6°.

claims.claim: M-scaling the stimulus reduced, but did not eliminate the HVA magnitude in peak contrast sensitivity.

claims.claim: The HVA magnitude in AULCSF did not change between 2° and 6°.

claims.claim: M-scaling reduced the HVA magnitude in AULCSF, but the HVA was still evident in the 6° M-scale condition.

claims.claim: The VMA magnitude in AULCSF increased between 2° and 6°.

results.result: Visual performance and contrast sensitivity decline with increasing eccentricity from the fovea to the periphery. Contrast sensitivity is bandpass near the fovea, peaking at approximately 4 cycles per degree, and decreases with eccentricity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C9, and C10 are well-established findings in vision science, supported by multiple citations to prior work (Campbell and Robson, 1968; Watson and Ahumada, 2005; Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Robson and Graham, 1981; Wright and Johnston, 1983). These claims represent foundational knowledge in the field and are not contested in the manuscript.

results.result: Contrast sensitivity exhibits robust polar angle asymmetries: it is higher along the horizontal meridian than the vertical meridian (HVA) and higher along the lower vertical meridian than the upper vertical meridian (VMA). These asymmetries depend on eccentricity, spatial frequency, and stimulus size, and persist across various stimulus manipulations, viewing conditions, and attentional states. The asymmetries are retinotopic rather than spatiotopic.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C11-C26 are extensively supported by multiple citations to prior work (Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001, 2022; Hanning et al., 2022a,b; Himmelberg et al., 2020, 2022b; Pointer and Hess, 1989; Rosén et al., 2014; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011; and many others). These claims establish the well-documented phenomenon of polar angle asymmetries in contrast sensitivity, which forms the foundation for the current study's investigation.

results.result: Perceptual asymmetries have been related to optical, retinal, and cortical factors. Cortical magnification, defined as the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm²/°), declines with eccentricity and has been used to link perceptual performance to brain structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 are supported by multiple citations to prior work (Kupers et al., 2019, 2022; Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2021, 2022b, 2023a; Silva et al., 2018; Engel et al., 1994; Horton and Hoyt, 1991; Van Essen et al., 1984; Duncan and Boynton, 2003; Schwarzkopf et al., 2011; Schwarzkopf and Rees, 2013; Song et al., 2015). These claims establish the theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between cortical magnification and perceptual performance.

results.result: For many visual tasks, magnifying stimulus size to equate the cortical representation eliminates performance differences at different eccentricities, supporting the 'quantitative hypothesis' that performance decline with eccentricity is due to decreasing neural count. However, performance does not successfully scale for several higher-order visual tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 are supported by multiple citations to prior work (Anton-Erxleben and Carrasco, 2013; Carrasco et al., 1998; Carrasco and Frieder, 1997; Kitterle, 1986; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979; Strasburger et al., 2011; Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Koenderink et al., 1978; Rovamo et al., 1978; Virsu and Rovamo, 1979; Hubel and Wiesel, 1977; Rockel et al., 1980). These claims establish the theoretical framework distinguishing the quantitative and qualitative hypotheses that the study aims to test.

results.result: Ten observers performed an orientation discrimination task with gratings at different eccentricities (2° and 6°) and polar angles (horizontal and vertical meridians), with both fixed-size and M-scaled stimuli. Grating contrast and spatial frequency varied on each trial, with contrast titrated using adaptive procedures targeting 75% performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43, C180-C195 describe the experimental design and methods in detail. The methods are clearly described, including sample size (n=10), stimulus parameters (spatial frequencies: 0.5-11.3 cpd; eccentricities: 2° and 6°; M-scaled sizes: 7.08°-7.70°), experimental procedures (fixation monitoring, trial structure, feedback), and titration procedures (best PEST and 3-down, 1-up staircase). The methods appear appropriate for the research question.

results.result: A parametric contrast sensitivity model was developed and fit to group-level data, incorporating a logistic contrast response function, nine candidate CSF models, and six visual field models. Model comparisons identified the YQM model as the best-fitting CSF model and 'Ecc + HVA + VMA' as the best-fitting visual field model.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C201 describe the modeling approach and results. The parametric model is well-specified (Equations 7-8, Tables 1-2), and model comparisons using BIC are appropriate. The identification of the YQM model and 'Ecc + HVA + VMA' visual field model as best-fitting is supported by Figure 3 and Tables 1-2. The modeling approach is rigorous and appropriate for the data.

results.result: Contrast sensitivity functions (CSFs) decline between the parafovea (2°) and perifovea (6°) for fixed-sized gratings, but M-scaling eliminates or reverses these differences at low and medium spatial frequencies. M-scaling diminished the eccentricity effect differentially across spatial frequency, with significant reductions for spatial frequencies 0.5-4 cpd but not for the highest spatial frequencies (8 and 11 cpd) which reached the acuity limit.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C55 are supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4A-B and statistical analyses (repeated-measures ANOVA: F(7,63) = 61.13, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.872; post hoc t-tests with appropriate p-values). The findings are consistent with prior work (Rovamo et al., 1978; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979) as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The statistical analyses are appropriate and the results are clearly presented.

results.result: The horizontal-vertical anisotropy (HVA) in contrast sensitivity remained after M-scaling. M-scaling reduced the HVA extent as a function of spatial frequency, but for all but one spatial frequency (8 cpd), M-scaling did not significantly affect the HVA. This finding supports the 'qualitative hypothesis' that the HVA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4C-D and statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA: F(7,63) = 7.32, p=0.0035, ηG2 = 0.449; post hoc t-tests). The finding that M-scaling does not eliminate the HVA is a key result supporting the qualitative hypothesis. The statistical analyses are appropriate, though the exception at 8 cpd (p=0.021) warrants further investigation. The interpretation (C62) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: The vertical meridian asymmetry (VMA) in contrast sensitivity remained after M-scaling. A two-way ANOVA found a main effect of spatial frequency on VMA extent but no main effect of stimulus size or interaction effect, indicating no difference in VMA extent before and after M-scaling. This finding supports the 'qualitative hypothesis' that the VMA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C71 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4E-F and statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA: F(7,63) = 10.16, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.53 for main effect of SF; no main effect of stimulus size or interaction, p>0.1). The finding that M-scaling does not eliminate the VMA is a key result supporting the qualitative hypothesis. The statistical analyses are appropriate and the interpretation (C71) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: The HVA in peak contrast sensitivity emerged only in the perifovea, whereas the VMA emerged at both eccentricities (2° and 6°). M-scaling matched peak contrast sensitivity between the parafovea and perifovea but did not equate contrast sensitivity around polar angle.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C79 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-B and statistical analyses (repeated-measures ANOVAs with appropriate F-statistics, p-values, and effect sizes; post hoc t-tests with 95% CIs and Cohen's d). The differential emergence of HVA and VMA in peak contrast sensitivity is clearly demonstrated. The statistical analyses are rigorous and appropriate.

results.result: The HVA and VMA emerged in cutoff spatial frequency. M-scaling reduced but did not eliminate the HVA in cutoff spatial frequency, and did not eliminate the VMA or the eccentricity effect. M-scaling did not equate cutoff spatial frequency among polar angles.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C90 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5C-D and statistical analyses (repeated-measures ANOVAs with appropriate F-statistics, p-values, and effect sizes; post hoc t-tests with 95% CIs and Cohen's d). The findings are consistent with previous studies (Barbot et al., 2021; Wilkinson et al., 2016). The statistical analyses are rigorous and the results clearly demonstrate that M-scaling does not eliminate polar angle asymmetries in cutoff spatial frequency.

results.result: The HVA in AULCSF was evident in both the parafovea and perifovea, and M-scaling did not eliminate it. The VMA in AULCSF was only evident in the perifovea, and M-scaling did not eliminate it.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5E-F and statistical analyses (repeated-measures ANOVAs with appropriate F-statistics, p-values, and effect sizes; post hoc t-tests with 95% CIs and Cohen's d). The findings for AULCSF are consistent with the results for peak contrast sensitivity and cutoff spatial frequency, further supporting the qualitative hypothesis. The statistical analyses are rigorous and appropriate.

results.result: The magnitude of the HVA and VMA varied across the three key CSF parameters (peak contrast sensitivity, cutoff spatial frequency, and AULCSF) and across eccentricities. M-scaling reduced but did not eliminate the HVA magnitude for peak contrast sensitivity, cutoff spatial frequency, and AULCSF. M-scaling did not alter the VMA magnitude for peak contrast sensitivity, cutoff spatial frequency, or AULCSF.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C109 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6 and statistical analyses (one-way ANOVAs with appropriate F-statistics and p-values; post hoc t-tests with 95% CIs). The quantification of asymmetry magnitudes provides additional evidence that M-scaling does not eliminate polar angle asymmetries. The statistical analyses are appropriate and the results are clearly presented.

results.result: M-scaling stimulus size based on its cortical representation eliminates differences in contrast sensitivity as a function of eccentricity, but not polar angle. This indicates that limits in contrast sensitivity across eccentricity and around polar angle of the visual field are mediated by different anatomical and computational constraints.
results.evaluation: Claims C110, C6, C7, and C8 represent the main findings of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental data and statistical analyses presented in Figures 4-6. The differential effects of M-scaling on eccentricity versus polar angle are clearly demonstrated across multiple CSF parameters (peak contrast sensitivity, cutoff spatial frequency, AULCSF). The conclusion that different constraints mediate eccentricity and polar angle effects is well-supported by the data.

results.result: fMRI measurements from 7 of 10 observers showed that V1 surface area is greater for the horizontal meridian than vertical meridian, and greater for the lower vertical meridian than upper vertical meridian. Individual differences in V1 surface area correlated with contrast sensitivity measurements at 6° and 6° M-scale, but not at 2°. However, the difference in contrast sensitivity after M-scaling did not correlate with V1 surface area.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C119 and C202 are supported by fMRI data presented in Figure 7 and statistical analyses (paired t-tests for group-level differences; Spearman's correlations for individual differences). The correlations between V1 surface area and contrast sensitivity at 6° (r = 0.40, p=0.036) and 6° M-scale (r = 0.39, p=0.040) are statistically significant, though modest. The lack of correlation at 2° (r = 0.16, p=0.400) and for the difference after M-scaling (r = 0.20, p=0.393) is also clearly reported. The sample size for fMRI (n=7) is smaller than the behavioral sample (n=10), which may limit statistical power.

results.result: The finding that M-scaling does not correct for the cortical representation at the horizontal meridian, lower vertical meridian, and upper vertical meridian supports the 'qualitative hypothesis' that there are additional underlying neural and computational factors beyond V1 cortical magnification that contribute to perceptual polar angle asymmetries.
results.evaluation: Claims C120, C121, C62, and C71 represent the main interpretation of the study's findings. The qualitative hypothesis is well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data showing that M-scaling eliminates eccentricity effects but not polar angle asymmetries. The interpretation is reasonable given the data, though the specific nature of the additional neural and computational factors remains to be determined in future work.

results.result: Cortical magnification limits peripheral vision, as evidenced by correlations between V1 surface area and perceptual measures across eccentricity. M-scaling stimulus size diminished the difference in contrast sensitivity and acuity between 2° and 6°, indicating that cortical magnification predominantly underlies performance differences as a function of eccentricity.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C128 are supported by the current study's findings and multiple citations to prior work (Duncan and Boynton, 2003; Song et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2006; Schwarzkopf et al., 2011; Schwarzkopf and Rees, 2013). The interpretation that cortical magnification predominantly underlies eccentricity effects is well-supported by the data showing that M-scaling eliminates or reverses eccentricity effects at low and medium spatial frequencies.

results.result: The finding that M-scaling does not eliminate polar angle asymmetries is surprising given that perceptual asymmetries have been linked to V1 cortical magnification. Psychophysical measures of the HVA and VMA magnitude match the cortical HVA and VMA (~60% more V1 tissue for horizontal meridian than vertical meridian; ~25% more for lower vertical meridian than upper vertical meridian). Individual differences in contrast sensitivity correlate with V1 surface area at each meridian. Thus, M-scaling should in principle equate contrast sensitivity, but it does not.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C136 are supported by the current study's findings and multiple citations to prior work (Abrams et al., 2012; Himmelberg et al., 2020, 2022a,b; Barbot et al., 2021; Benson et al., 2021). The apparent paradox—that polar angle asymmetries correlate with cortical asymmetries but are not eliminated by M-scaling—is clearly articulated and forms the basis for the qualitative hypothesis. The interpretation is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Across the three key CSF parameters (peak contrast sensitivity, cutoff spatial frequency, and AULCSF), M-scaling stimulus size decreased the magnitude of the HVA and VMA, but did not eliminate the perceptual asymmetries. The asymmetries persisted after equating for their cortical representation.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C150 summarize the main findings across all CSF parameters. The summary is well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data and statistical analyses presented in Figures 4-6. The conclusion that asymmetries persist after equating for cortical representation is the key finding supporting the qualitative hypothesis.

results.result: Polar angle asymmetries have been identified for fundamental basic visual properties, mid-level properties, and higher-order properties. Contrast sensitivity is the currency of the visual system, which most visual dimensions depend upon. If M-scaling does not eliminate polar angle asymmetries at the most fundamental level, then it is unlikely to eliminate asymmetries for higher-order dimensions.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C155 are supported by multiple citations to prior work documenting polar angle asymmetries across various visual tasks. The speculation (C155) that M-scaling is unlikely to eliminate asymmetries for higher-order dimensions is reasonable given the current findings, though the authors appropriately note that this has yet to be empirically tested.

results.result: M-scaling stimulus size based on the cortical representation as a function of polar angle diminished but did not eliminate the HVA, and had no effect on the VMA. These findings suggest that performance differences as a function of polar angle are likely to be mediated by both the cortical representation and by differential computations or image-processing capabilities of these neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C158 represent the main conclusion of the study, well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data. The interpretation that both cortical representation and differential neural computations contribute to polar angle asymmetries is reasonable given the data, though the specific nature of these differential computations remains to be determined in future work.

results.result: Observers' viewing distance changed when stimuli were presented at the horizontal meridian versus vertical meridian for non-scaled stimuli, resulting in different monitor luminances (23 cd/m² and 19 cd/m², respectively). However, this change in luminance is not large enough to significantly affect contrast measurements, and asymmetries have been reported in many studies with constant viewing distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C162 address a potential methodological concern. The authors appropriately acknowledge the viewing distance difference and provide evidence (citation to Rahimi-Nasrabadi et al., 2021) that the luminance difference is not large enough to affect contrast measurements. The additional evidence from prior studies with constant viewing distance (multiple citations) further supports that the asymmetries are not artifacts of the viewing distance manipulation.

results.result: Perceptual asymmetries have been linked to V1 properties (surface area, population receptive field size, and BOLD amplitude) at both the group and individual level. Individual differences in contrast sensitivity in the current study correlate with individual differences in V1 surface area along the polar angle meridians. Thus, the asymmetries must be explained by cortical magnification to some extent.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C166 are supported by the current study's fMRI findings (Figure 7) and multiple citations to prior work (Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2021, 2022a,b; Liu et al., 2006; Moutsiana et al., 2016; O'Connell et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2018). The inference (C166) that cortical magnification must explain the asymmetries to some extent is reasonable given the correlations, though the lack of correlation for the difference after M-scaling (C119) suggests that cortical magnification alone is insufficient.

results.result: M-scaling has been shown to work for fundamental visual dimensions and fail for more complex dimensions. Critically, the current study found that for the same visual task and dimension (contrast sensitivity), M-scaling works for certain locations (eccentricity) but fails for others (cardinal polar angles).
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C169 are supported by multiple citations to prior work and the current study's findings. The key insight (C169) that M-scaling works for eccentricity but not polar angle within the same task is a novel and important contribution, clearly demonstrated by the experimental data.

results.result: Between-subject variability in the V1 polar angle representation may underlie the inability of M-scaling to extinguish perceptual polar angle asymmetries. There is substantial variability in V1 size and tissue distribution. There may be greater variability in the cortical representation of polar angle compared to eccentricity that is not accounted for by M-scaling equations derived from group-level data. Even if stimulus size were adjusted via M-scaling equations based on individualized V1 surface measures, the perceptual asymmetries would likely remain.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C174 are speculative explanations for why M-scaling does not eliminate polar angle asymmetries. While the variability in V1 size and tissue distribution is well-documented (citations to Benson et al., 2022; Dougherty et al., 2003; Himmelberg et al., 2022b; Moutsiana et al., 2016), the specific claim that this variability underlies the failure of M-scaling is not directly tested. The speculation (C174) that individualized M-scaling would also fail is based on the lack of correlation between V1 surface area and the change in contrast sensitivity after M-scaling (C119), which is suggestive but not definitive. These claims represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not conclusively supported by the current data.

results.result: Limits in contrast sensitivity across eccentricity and around polar angle likely emerge from different anatomical and computational constraints. The findings challenge the generalizability of the established view that cortical magnification limits basic visual perception throughout the visual field. Differences in contrast sensitivity at different eccentricities are predominantly mediated by cortical magnification, whereas differences as a function of polar angle must be constrained by additional computational and neural image-processing capabilities. Models of spatial vision linking brain and behavior should account for what constrains basic visual perception not only across but also around the visual field.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C179 represent the main conclusions of the study. These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data showing differential effects of M-scaling on eccentricity versus polar angle. The challenge to the generalizability of cortical magnification as the sole explanation for visual field effects (C176) is justified by the data. The recommendation for future modeling work (C179) is appropriate given the findings.
